reason: Refuted on the wording, and specifically on the verifier's own correction, which runs the wrong way. The verifier inserted a that (whatever nonsensical thoughts THAT have entered my head) on the authority of the Wikipedia article on the Tsurezuregusa, and wrote a note saying the Columbia University Press text of Keene reads it that way and that quotation collections quietly drop the that. I fetched a course reader titled ESSAYS IN IDLENESS BY THE TSUREZUREGUSA OF KENKO, SELECTIONS TRANSLATED BY DONALD KEENE, extracted its text this run, and its first line of running text, the Preface entire, reads: What a strange, demented feeling it gives me when I realize I have spent whole days before this inkstone, with nothing better to do, jotting down at random whatever nonsensical thoughts have entered my head. No that. The reader is a straight transcription of Keene and carries his numbered sections and his footnotes on Fujiwara no Sanesada and Saigyo, so it is his text and not a collection's paraphrase. A second, independent check of the wording agrees with the reading without that. The reading with that is also ungrammatical English after whatever, which Keene would not have written. So the direction of the verifier's fix is reversed: Wikipedia is the outlier that added the word, the collections are right, and the verifier's note asserts the opposite as fact while admitting in the same breath that no copy of the printing was opened. That is the failure the standard forbids, a confident claim about an edition nobody read, and it puts an altered word inside quotation marks. Everything else about the line is sound and it should ship on the corrected wording: shipped.js reports not shipped, nothing near, Yoshida Kenkō at 1 of 3 for the year (month 3), not banned, and no Kenkō in the October carry list; the Preface is the right locator and the whole of it; Essay is the form of the work, a zuihitsu; the source line is 90 characters, leads with the name, has no dash and no straight quote; scope and publishability are clean and the fit for a month of stillness is exact. One residual caveat the note should carry honestly: the reader I read does not state a printing year, so 1967 rests on the edition history of the Columbia volume rather than on a scan of the 1967 printing, and the 1998 reissue is the text Wikipedia cites.
